title: Look to others (Philippians 1:27–2:4)
hook: do nothing out of selfish ambition; look to others' interests

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man in chains wrote to live is Christ, and to die is gain. Your line was to live is christ. What good did you find inside your constraint? Day six hundred fifty-nine.

Philippi was proud of being Roman. It was a colony, settled by veterans of Rome's wars, and its citizens had the rights of people living in Rome itself, even though they were hundreds of miles away in Greece. Latin on the inscriptions. Roman law in the courts. In the book of Acts, the crowd there accuses Paul of teaching customs that Romans aren't allowed to keep. So when Paul writes to the church in Philippi about how to live, he reaches for a word every one of them knew. The word for being a citizen.

The King James Bible says: "Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ." Conversation, in old English, meant your whole way of life, not just talk. But Paul's Greek word is politeuesthe: live as citizens. Behave as citizens worthy of the good news. Later in the letter he'll say their real citizenship is in heaven. So: you know how to be Roman. Now be citizens of something else, together. Then he asks for something hard, and he asks it warmly. If there's any comfort in Christ, any fellowship of the Spirit, any tenderness, then "Fulfil ye my joy, that ye be likeminded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind." Make my joy complete by getting along. It seems the Philippians had some friction; later he names two women who need to agree. Then the heart of it: "Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves." Vainglory is empty glory: doing things to look good. Lowliness of mind is humility, a word the Greek world often used as an insult, meaning servile, low. Paul makes it a virtue. And then: "Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others." Notice that small word: also. Paul doesn't say ignore your own needs. He says don't stop at them. Look at your own things, and also at the things of others. It's a picture of a community where everyone is quietly watching out for someone else, and someone else is watching out for them. And tomorrow, Paul gives the reason: the pattern of Christ himself.
screen: `MAKE MY JOY COMPLETE: BE OF ONE MIND.`
`NO EMPTY GLORY; HUMILITY AS A VIRTUE.`
then, large: `LOOK NOT EVERY MAN ON HIS OWN THINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put someone's interest first. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people you'll be around today: at home, at work, in line, online. Pick one. What do they need today that you could notice? The last good parking spot. The chance to finish their story. Credit for their idea in a meeting. The bigger slice. Choose one specific way to put their interest ahead of yours, without making a show of it. If you pray, you can ask for eyes to see what others need. The bell holds the time.
Look to others. Paul's plea to a proud Roman colony: no empty glory, humility instead, and an eye on the needs of the people around you.
Your line: others first. Today, do the one specific thing you chose, and don't mention that you did it. Day six hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Many Christian communities take Philippians 2:3–4 as a rule for their life together, and it is often read when churches, families or teams are working through conflict.

fork.setup: you're writing to a church that's proud of its Roman citizenship, and there's friction among them. what picture do you reach for?
options: tell them to stop being Roman.
tell them to live as citizens worthy of the gospel.
tell them to choose a leader to settle it.
fork.reveal: Paul uses their own civic word, politeuesthe: live as citizens, worthy of the gospel, of one mind.

original.note: Greek: live as citizens. from polis, city. the KJV renders it 'let your conversation be'.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rule to put yourself last.
what it means: in a proud Roman colony, live as citizens of something else: no empty glory, and an eye on others' needs as well as your own.
what a scholar hears: politeuesthe in 1:27 and politeuma in 3:20, and tapeinophrosyne, humility, a word with a low reputation in Greek ethics that Paul turns into a virtue.

notes: Philippi as a Roman colony settled by veterans (after 42 and 31 BC), with ius Italicum. Script says 'rights of people living in Rome itself' as a simplification. Confirm.
'Fulfil' is KJV spelling inside a quotation.
Humility (tapeinos) as a mostly negative word in Greek ethics: common observation; stated as 'often'. Confirm.
The note on 'also' in 2:4: the word kai is present in most manuscripts; confirm.
Mention of 'two women who need to agree' points ahead to 4:2 (day 665) without naming them.
